challenges.headline: Editing a signed document
challenges.premise: The request treats a signed document as something managers can 'edit' and then re-approve, as if the edit were a change to the existing document.
challenges.alternative: Treat it as issuing a new version that supersedes the signed one. The signed version stays frozen, readable and referenceable, and the new version goes through approval (and signature if needed) on its own. If the real need is changing terms of a contract, a formal amendment may fit better than a free edit.
challenges.consequence: Building true in-place editing would break the audit trail and the validity of existing signatures, and anything pointing at the signed version (links, citations, prior signatures) would silently point at changed content. Building supersession is a larger job than the request sounds, and the client may not expect that scope.
challenges.recommendation: Confirm with the client that 'edit' means 'supersede with a new version', and ask whether the typical reason is correcting errors or changing terms, since those may deserve different paths.

challenges.headline: Build before trying configuration
challenges.premise: The request assumes a new capability is needed, although the platform already has versioning and approval circuits.
challenges.alternative: Check first whether a new version routed through a configured re-approval circuit already covers most of the need. The remaining work might then be a rule change (allowing managers to start a new version of a signed document) rather than a new feature.
challenges.consequence: Without this check the team may build a second approval path that duplicates existing circuits, and that has to be maintained next to them.
challenges.recommendation: Before estimating, run the scenario end to end on the existing versioning and approval circuits and list exactly what falls short.

challenges.headline: Managers as sole initiators
challenges.premise: Managers are the people who edit, and by implication they have enough authority to drive the change.
challenges.alternative: Let managers request or draft the new version, but keep re-approval with someone other than the editor (the original approvers or a higher level). This keeps segregation of duties without limiting who can start a change.
challenges.consequence: If a manager can edit and also approve their own change, the re-approval adds no control, and the audit trail loses most of its value for compliance.
challenges.recommendation: Decide who re-approves and whether the editor is excluded, before designing the circuit.

challenges.headline: Edit in place vs supersede
challenges.premise: The request says managers should 'edit' documents after they are signed, which reads as changing the signed document itself.
challenges.alternative: Treat every post-signature change as a new version that supersedes the signed one. The signed version stays frozen and referenceable, and the new version carries its own approval and signature. This is an assumption we have made; the client has not confirmed it.
challenges.consequence: Altering a signed version in place would destroy the evidence of what was actually signed, break links and citations that point at that version, and weaken the audit trail and e-signature validity. It would also contradict the platform's frozen-after-approval rule.
challenges.recommendation: Confirm with the client that 'edit' means 'issue a new version' before any design work, and state explicitly that the signed original is never altered.

challenges.headline: One flow for every change
challenges.premise: Every change to a signed document, from a typo to a changed amount, needs the same edit-and-re-approve treatment.
challenges.alternative: Separate light corrections (typos, formatting) from substantive amendments (amounts, terms, dates). Corrections could follow a shorter circuit, and substantive changes would trigger full re-approval and re-signature. Which categories exist is for the client to define; this is a proposal only.
challenges.consequence: A single heavy flow either burdens managers with full re-signature for trivial fixes, which defeats the purpose of the request, or lets substantive changes through a path that is too light to be defensible at audit.
challenges.recommendation: Ask managers for a sample of recent real cases and what changed in each before fixing the approval and signature rules.

challenges.headline: Managers as sole editors and approvers
challenges.premise: Managers both edit signed documents and re-approve them, with the approval circuit left unspecified.
challenges.alternative: Let managers initiate the change but route approval to someone other than the author, such as the original approvers or a higher level. A manager would never approve their own change. This is a proposal, as the client has not stated who should re-approve.
challenges.consequence: If a manager can edit and approve their own change to a signed document, the re-approval adds no control, and an auditor can challenge it as a lack of segregation of duties.
challenges.recommendation: Decide with the client who approves and whether the author can ever be an approver, before sizing the permissions work.

decisions.decision: An audit trail of every change is required.
decisions.why: Changing already-signed documents is exactly where auditability is examined, and retrofitting it later is expensive.

open_decisions: Does 'edit' mean a new version superseding the signed one, or do they expect in-place change?
Must the original signatories sign again, or is re-approval enough?
Which version is current while the new one is pending?
Who re-approves, and can a manager approve their own change?
Which document types, clients and managers are in scope?
What legal, retention or audit obligations apply?
What triggers this today, and what kinds of changes are involved?
How will success be judged, and what is the deadline?
How are documents already signed or in flight handled at go-live?

briefs.problem: Signed documents sometimes need to change, but the request does not say why (errors, changed terms, periodic updates), and the platform treats signed content as frozen.
briefs.solution: A supersession flow: a manager starts a new version from a signed document, which goes through approval and re-signature, while the signed original is retained and marked superseded, with a full audit trail.
introduces: a supersession flow that creates a new version from a signed one and links it to the original
a new manager right to reopen signed documents, scoped by role and classification
re-approval and re-signature rules, including segregation of duties
rules for which version is current while a re-approval is pending
reconciliation of links, citations and downstream consumers that point at the superseded version

challenges.headline: Edit signed documents in place
challenges.premise: The request says managers 'edit' documents after signature, which reads as changing the signed content itself.
challenges.alternative: Treat every post-signature change as a new version. The signed version stays untouched and referenceable, and the new version goes through approval and signature. This is my reading of the request; the client has not confirmed it.
challenges.consequence: An in-place edit would break the validity of the existing signatures and leave gaps in the audit trail. Anything that cites the signed version would silently point at changed content.
challenges.recommendation: Confirm with the client that 'edit' means 'supersede with a new version', and that overwriting signed content is not what they want.

challenges.headline: Managers re-approving their own edits
challenges.premise: The request puts edit and re-approve in the same role, which implies the manager who changes the document also validates it.
challenges.alternative: Separate the editor from the re-approver. The re-approval would go through a circuit that excludes the editor and may use different approvers than the original round. Whether this is required is an open question, not something the client has said.
challenges.consequence: If editing and approving sit with one person, the approval step guards nothing. It would also undermine the audit trail and could weaken the credibility of the re-signature.
challenges.recommendation: Ask the client who must re-approve and re-sign, and whether the editing manager may take part. Decide this before designing the circuit.

challenges.headline: Building before checking existing capability
challenges.premise: The request assumes a new capability is needed.
challenges.alternative: The platform already has versioning, approval circuits and signature. The need may be met largely by configuring those, with a small addition such as a 'create a new version from a signed one' action and a manager permission.
challenges.consequence: Building a bespoke flow could duplicate existing machinery and add a parallel path to maintain, and the audit and permission rules would have to be kept consistent across both.
challenges.recommendation: Before estimating, walk through how a signed document is corrected today and what the existing versioning and circuits already do. List only the gaps.

complexity_reasons: supersession across two lifecycles (approval/signature and publication)
re-approval circuits that vary by client
classification-driven permissions and segregation of duties
audit trail with no gaps across old and new versions
briefs.cost_driver: supersession semantics: signature handling and which version is current during re-approval
risks: People acting on the wrong version while a re-approval is pending, because 'current' is not defined (latest, latest approved, or latest published).
Existing signatures may be invalidated or need re-collecting, which could break downstream processes that relied on the original signature.
Legal signature validity, retention and audit obligations could restrict or forbid post-signature changes for some document types or classifications.
Approval circuits and permission rules are shared across modules, so a new manager right may affect several screens.
Already-signed documents and links pointing at them need a migration and reconciliation path.

opportunities.text: Build supersession as a generic 'new version from a frozen version' capability rather than a manager-only feature.
Make the re-approval circuit and the right to reopen configurable per client, reusing the existing client-specific approval circuits.
Provide a single resolver for 'current document' that other features such as search, listings, notifications and export can share.

next_steps: Run a short discovery with the client on the six open points: supersession versus in-place edit, current version during re-approval, who re-approves, how corrections are done today, documents that must never change, and per-client variation.
Map what existing versioning, approval circuits and signature already cover and list only the gaps, before estimating.
Confirm legal signature validity and retention constraints with compliance, by document type and classification.
Estimate and build a narrow first slice once decided: new version from a signed one, re-approval with an editor-excluded circuit, old version stamped superseded, audit trail.

decisions.decision: Treat a post-signature change as a new version, never an in-place edit, with the signed version retained and referenceable
decisions.why: The platform's document model freezes approved and signed versions, and the audit trail and signature validity depend on that.
decisions.alternative: Overwrite the signed content in place.
decisions.tradeoff: More build and a clearer version history, in exchange for intact signatures and an audit trail without gaps.

decisions.decision: The audit trail must record who changed what, previous versus new value, and who re-approved and when
decisions.why: Changing signed records is a compliance matter, so auditability is a hard requirement.

open_decisions: Is the change a new version (supersession) or an in-place edit?
Which version is current while re-approval is pending: the old signed one or the new one?
Who must re-approve and re-sign, and may the editing manager take part?
What happens to existing signatures: invalidated, or re-collected?
Which documents or classifications must never be changed after signature?
Is the behaviour the same for all clients or configurable per client?
How are signed documents corrected today, and what existing capability already covers it?
Success criteria and acceptance scenarios for the feature
Who is notified when a signed document is reopened or superseded, and do downstream systems rely on the signature event?
